To: group:levy-longsight-noticeboard
Replying to: none
Cc: none
Subject: Please read and share: fake blue pills, and what to do if someone goes down

I know there's a lot of talk on here at the moment. I'm not going to add to it, and I won't be answering questions about anyone or anything that's happened, so please don't ask. I just want to make sure everyone has seen this, because the police warning has been up since Thursday and I don't think many people have read it.

Blue tablets are being sold round south Manchester as diazepam or "Xanax". Some of them have been found to contain nitazenes. These are synthetic opioids and they can be far stronger than heroin. Whoever's taking them has no idea what's actually in them, and the person selling them probably doesn't either.

What to look out for (from the police post):
- extreme drowsiness, can't stay awake or can't be woken
- pinpoint pupils (the black dot in the middle of the eye goes really tiny)
- slow or noisy breathing, snoring or gurgling sounds
- blue or grey lips

If you see any of that, RING 999 STRAIGHT AWAY.

This is the bit I really need people to hear. What often happens, and this is general and not about anybody, is that mates panic. They don't want anyone getting in trouble, so they put the person to bed to "sleep it off" and maybe ring for help hours later. With opioids, sleeping it off is how people die. Their breathing slows down and down, and by the time someone rings, the brain has gone without oxygen for too long. Snoring is not a sign they're fine. If you're not sure, ring anyway. Nobody will be cross with you for ringing over nothing.

While you wait for the ambulance, stay with them, put them on their side, and keep talking to them. Do what the call handler tells you.

Don't worry about getting in trouble. The police have literally said in their own post: "Our priority is preserving life." Ringing for help is what they want you to do. Please tell your kids this in those exact words if you need to.

Naloxone: there's a nasal spray that can reverse an opioid overdose long enough for help to arrive. You can get it FREE from Brightpath drug & alcohol service on Stockport Road (next to the launderette). Anyone can ask for one and they don't need your name. The training takes about 10 minutes. They're open Monday to Friday 10-4, and Thursdays until 7. If you've got teenagers, older kids who go out, or anyone in the house who might use, please think about getting one. It's a little thing to have in a drawer.

Talk to your kids THIS WEEK. Not after half term or when you get round to it. I had the chat with my lad (he's 14) last night over his tea. I got the eye rolls, but he listened, and he asked me what pinpoint pupils meant, so something went in. It doesn't need to be a big sit-down lecture. Tell them pills going round might not be what they say they are, what the signs look like, and that if a mate goes down they ring 999 and they will NOT be in trouble with you for doing it.

And please, can we stop slagging the kids off. I get that people are angry and scared, but it doesn't help. Scared kids don't ring for help. They hide it, and that's the whole problem. If teenagers think they'll be judged or punished, they'll put their mate to bed instead of picking up the phone. We need them to know that ringing is always the right thing to do, whatever they've taken and whatever trouble they think they're in.

Please SHARE this, don't just like it. Share it to your own page, your school WhatsApp groups, your family chats, anywhere teenagers or their parents will see it. If it gets to one kid who then knows what to do, it's worth it.

Thanks for reading. Look after each other x

Becky

reasons: The draft says the police warning has been up since Thursday, but the supplied post is dated Friday.
